newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Britain condemns IRA truce "blackmail".
newsitem.headline: Britain condemns IRA truce "blackmail".

text.p: Britain said it would not bow to IRA blackmail on Friday after the Irish guerrillas dashed hopes of an early ceasefire in a war against London's rule over Northern Ireland.

The Irish Republican Army leadership was reported to have ruled out any new truce until after an impending British election in the hope that a new government will give its Sinn Fein political wing a seat at peace talks.

On the eve of the first anniversary of the collapse of a historic 17-month guerrilla truce, a source close to the IRA's leadership said British Prime Minister John Major's refusal to ease terms for Sinn Fein's entry to the talks ruled out any immediate new IRA ceasefire.
"At the present there is no sign of a meaningful move from the British and in that event there is no immediate sign of a ceasefire," the source told Dublin journalists.
Britain, due to have a general election by late May, gave a withering response.

"It implies that after the election it may be kind enough to announce another ceasefire. But by those words, they surely show themselves to be the blackmailers they are," Northern Ireland Secretary, Sir Patrick Mayhew told BBC radio.
"In a democracy that will never wash and will never be allowed to wash," he added.
But leading nationalist peace-broker John Hume made an impassioned plea to the IRA to abandon violence and put trust in peace talks.

"My appeal to you now is - have faith in all of us. Lay down your weapons and let the British and Irish governments and the representatives of the Irish people come together to bring about agreement," Social Democratic and Labour Party leader Hume said at at a public function in Dublin.

Hume, who has maintained contact with Gerry Adams, head of the IRA's political wing, in a bid to bring about a truce, insisted that in spite of pervading gloom "we still have the best opportunity to remove the gun forever from Irish politics."
A massive bomb that killed two civilians at London's Canary Wharf business complex a year ago heralded the IRA's return to war and threw an Anglo-Irish peace process into chaos.
Martin McGuinness, Sinn Fein's chief negotiator, told BBC radio he was "heartened" by the fact that the IRA statement said the guerrillas wanted to see a negotiated settlement.
But he said it would require a British leader of the stature of former South African President F.W. de Klerk to find a solution to Europe's longest guerrilla war.

The IRA abandoned the truce accusing Britain of blocking Sinn Fein's entry to the talks by insisting that progress be made on dismantling the guerrillas' armoury, which includes Semtex plastic explosive and sophisticated assault weaponry.
The London government says the Canary Wharf bombing, which killed two people, proved the IRA's truce was a tactical ploy.
It says the IRA must declare a genuine ceasefire before Sinn Fein is allowed to join other parties at talks that have made slow headway since June. Sinn Fein demands unconditional entry.
The IRA has stepped up attacks on the province's security forces with a series of mortar and grenade attacks.
